utterance: Hi Daniel, I'm the GP today. I see from the booking note that you hurt your lower back over the weekend and it's giving you a hard time. Can you tell me what happened and how it's feeling now?
reply: I was lifting a big pot plant in the garden on Saturday, felt a twinge, and then woke up Sunday and could barely get out of bed, so it has been about three days now. It is low down on the left side of my back, and sometimes it goes into my left buttock. It is worse when I bend or get out of a chair, but better lying still with a heat pack, and it definitely gets worse by the evening. I have worked from home the last two days, mostly lying on the couch with the laptop, and I can walk around slowly.

utterance:
I have good news for you, Daniel. Based on your story and my examination today, you have acute non-specific mechanical low back pain—essentially a strain and spasm of the muscles and supporting structures in the left side of your lower back from lifting that heavy pot plant.

Importantly, there are no warning signs of any serious spinal problem or nerve root compression: your leg strength, reflexes, and sensation are all completely normal, and pressing on the spine itself is comfortable.

Regarding the MRI scan you asked about: in cases like yours where there are no nerve symptoms or warning signs, clinical guidelines actually recommend against doing an MRI or X-ray early on. That's because scans don't change how we treat acute back strain, they won't help you recover faster, and they often show normal age-related wear-and-tear findings that have nothing to do with your current pain and can cause unnecessary worry. The vast majority of acute back strains settle down really well over the next couple of weeks without needing any scans or surgery.

To help you get through this week and meet your work deadline comfortably, here is what I recommend:
1. Stay gently active: Try to avoid lying flat on the couch for long periods, as prolonged bed rest actually stiffens the back and slows recovery. Keep walking gently around the house, change positions every 20 to 30 minutes when working at your desk, and return to your normal activities as pain allows.
2. Keep using the heat pack on your lower back, as superficial heat is great for relaxing muscle spasm.
3. For pain relief: Paracetamol alone isn't very effective for back pain. Instead, a short course of an anti-inflammatory tablet like ibuprofen (400 mg up to three times a day with food for 5 to 7 days) works much better to settle the pain so you can keep moving. We avoid strong opioid painkillers (especially as you're allergic to tramadol anyway) as they aren't helpful for back strain.
4. If it's still a bit stiff after a week or two, seeing a physiotherapist for gentle exercises and lifting advice can be really helpful, though most people improve steadily over 1 to 2 weeks.

Finally, just as a safety net: please seek urgent medical attention (or go straight to the emergency department) if you develop any new warning signs, such as numbness around your groin or bottom, any difficulty passing urine or controlling your bladder or bowels, weakness or numbness in your legs, severe pain shooting down your legs, or fevers. Otherwise, if things aren't clearly improving in 2 to 4 weeks, come back and see me for a review.

How does that plan sound to you, and do you have any questions?
reply: Are you sure I don't need a scan? I'm just really worried it's a slipped disc given how badly it hurts to move.

awards.label: Ibuprofen 400 mg orally three times daily with food, short course

utterance: I completely understand why it feels alarming—muscle spasm in the lower back is the body's way of splinting the area, and the pain from a simple muscle and ligament strain can be surprisingly severe when you try to bend or get out of a chair. However, when a disc slips and presses on a nerve, it causes shooting electric-like pain down the leg into the calf or foot, and shows up on the nerve tests we just did (like raising your straight leg or testing your ankle reflexes and foot strength). Because your leg raise was completely free of leg pain and all your nerve tests are 100% normal, we can be very confident that your nerves are safe and healthy. Even if we did an MRI today, it frequently picks up minor incidental disc bulges that exist in most healthy 40-year-olds with zero back pain, which only causes more anxiety without helping you heal. If your pain doesn't improve as expected over the next 4 to 6 weeks, or if any nerve symptoms ever appear, we can always reconsider a scan then. I've put through a script for ibuprofen 400 mg tablets to take with food up to three times daily for a few days. Does that help put your mind at ease?
reply: That makes sense, and I am glad my nerves are okay. I will pick up those tablets and try to stay moving.

awards.label: Correct diagnosis: Acute non-specific low back pain
